findings.title: Unsigned executable/library
findings.description: This binary carries no Authenticode signature, so its origin and integrity cannot be cryptographically verified. Unsigned binaries are easier to tamper with or substitute without detection, and are often flagged by endpoint security and SmartScreen.
findings.remediation: Sign all shipped executables and libraries with a valid code-signing certificate from a trusted CA, and verify signatures as part of the build/release pipeline.
findings.poc:
1. Confirm no signature is present directly:
     Windows (PowerShell):
       Get-AuthenticodeSignature -FilePath "C:\Users\ankes\Downloads\Network VAPT Reporting Tool.exe" | Format-List
       (Status will show 'NotSigned')
     Linux:
       osslsigncode verify "C:\Users\ankes\Downloads\Network VAPT Reporting Tool.exe"
       (Output will show 'No signature found')

2. Impact demonstration: because there is no signature, Windows SmartScreen/AppLocker/WDAC publisher-based rules cannot distinguish this binary from a tampered or malicious replacement. If this file sits in a writable location (cross-reference any writable-directory finding for the same path), an attacker's replacement binary would be indistinguishable from the original at the OS trust level.

3. For the client report: capture the Get-AuthenticodeSignature output as evidence alongside a screenshot of the file's Properties > Digital Signatures tab in Windows Explorer (which will show no 'Digital Signatures' tab at all for an unsigned file).

findings.title: High-entropy string (possible unrecognized secret)
findings.description: A string with unusually high randomness (Shannon entropy) was found, which often indicates an API key, token, or password that doesn't match a known vendor pattern. (Extracted from embedded strings inside a PE binary.)
findings.remediation: Manually review this value. If it is a credential or token, remove it from the file, rotate it, and load it via a secrets manager or environment variable instead.
findings.poc:
1. Extract printable strings from the binary directly to confirm independently:
   Windows (Sysinternals strings.exe):
     strings64.exe -n 6 "C:\Users\ankes\Downloads\Network VAPT Reporting Tool.exe" | findstr /i "PyMarsha"
   Linux:
     strings -n 6 "C:\Users\ankes\Downloads\Network VAPT Reporting Tool.exe" | grep -i 'PyMarsha'

2. Open Network VAPT Reporting Tool.exe in a PE viewer (CFF Explorer, Detect It Easy, or IDA/Ghidra) and locate the string in the resource/data section to confirm it is not dead code or a leftover debug string.

3. If confirmed live, treat this the same as a config-file secret: rotate the credential and remove it from the compiled binary — hardcoded strings in compiled code are trivially recoverable with basic reverse-engineering tools regardless of packing.

4. Evidence: PyMarshal_ReadObjectFromString

findings.title: Manifest privilege settings detected
findings.description: The embedded manifest declares the following privilege-affecting settings: requestedExecutionLevel="asInvoker", uiAccess="false". These values do not request elevated execution by default.
findings.remediation: Use the lowest required requestedExecutionLevel (asInvoker unless elevation is genuinely required), avoid autoElevate unless explicitly needed and properly signed/trusted, and ensure uiAccess is only enabled for approved assistive UI scenarios.
